rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling cramfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem is a free implementation of the Veritas filesystem and is the primary filesystem type used on HP-UX systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling freevxfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem that allows Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem designed to succeed hfs, enabling Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfsplus when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 (Journaling Flash File System 2) filesystem is a journaling filesystem designed for use on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling jffs2 when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The overlayfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The overlayfs kernel module (OverlayFS) provides a union-mount filesystem that combines an upper and lower filesystem into a single unified view.
rules.impact: The overlayfs kernel module has known CVEs: CVE-2023-32629, CVE-2023-2640, and CVE-2023-0386. Disabling unused OverlayFS support reduces the local attack surface and mitigates risks related to unauthorized setuid file execution.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A squashfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling squashfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf filesystem implements the Universal Disk Format (ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167), an open format used to store data on a wide range of media, including DVD and newer optical discs.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling udf when optical media support is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The USB storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: USB storage devices allow portable transfer and retention of files independent of network connectivity. Their widespread use has also made USB media a common vector for introducing malware and establishing persistent access.
rules.impact: Restricting USB storage access reduces the physical attack surface and limits a common path for malware introduction into the environment.

rules.title: Unused filesystem kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: Filesystem kernel modules extend the Linux kernel with support for additional filesystem types that can be loaded dynamically at runtime.
rules.impact: Unused filesystem modules expand the local attack surface. Attackers on a compromised system can abuse loadable filesystem modules to conceal processes or files; removing unnecessary filesystem support limits that risk.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary storage by users and applications.
rules.impact: Mounting /tmp as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, reducing the risk that an attacker can stage and run executable code from /tmp. It also helps prevent hard-link based attacks against setuid programs that may be updated on the system.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /tmp and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying nosuid prevents users from introducing setuid binaries in /tmp that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute malicious binaries staged in /tmp.

rules.title: /dev/shm is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /dev/shm directory is a world-writable shared-memory filesystem commonly used for inter-process communication (IPC).
rules.impact: Mounting /dev/shm as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, reducing the risk that an attacker can place and run executable code in shared memory. It also helps prevent hard-link based attacks against setuid programs.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /dev/shm is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating special devices on /dev/shm and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /dev/shm prevents introduction of privileged programs via shared memory that could be executed by non-root users, reducing privilege-escalation risk.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /dev/shm prevents execution of programs from shared memory, reducing the risk that users introduce and run malicious software from this location.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory provides disk space for local user data and home directories.
rules.impact: Default installations often place all data on a single root filesystem. Isolating /home on a separate partition contains user-driven disk growth and reduces the risk that resource exhaustion in /home will fill the root filesystem and disrupt overall system availability.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /home and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended for user files, applying nosuid prevents users from creating setuid binaries in /home that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and system services for dynamic and temporary data. Some directories under /var may be world-writable.
rules.impact: Placing /var on a separate partition enables additional mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage exploits. Isolation also helps contain growth of variable data so it does not exhaust the root filesystem.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is intended for variable data such as logs and service state, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary storage by users and applications. Unlike /tmp, files in /var/tmp are expected to persist across reboots.
rules.impact: Mounting /var/tmp as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage and execute exploits from temporary storage.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var/tmp and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying nosuid prevents users from introducing setuid binaries in /var/tmp that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute malicious binaries staged in /var/tmp.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: Mounting /var/log as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage exploits. Isolation also helps prevent log growth from exhausting the root filesystem.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var/log and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is intended only for log files, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var/log that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is intended only for log files, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute binaries staged under /var/log.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The audit daemon (auditd) stores its log data under the /var/log/audit directory.
rules.impact: Mounting /var/log/audit as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage exploits. Isolation also helps protect audit log capacity from being exhausted by unrelated filesystem activity.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log/audit is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var/log/audit and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log/audit is intended only for audit logs, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var/log/audit that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log/audit is intended only for audit logs, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute binaries staged under /var/log/audit.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: The files /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ define which APT repositories the system uses to obtain packages and security updates.
rules.impact: Incorrect repository configuration may prevent delivery of important security patches or allow untrusted repositories to introduce compromised software.

rules.title: The AppArmor package is installed
rules.explanation: AppArmor is a Mandatory Access Control (MAC) framework that confines processes according to per-application security profiles.
rules.impact: Without AppArmor, the system lacks this process confinement layer, increasing the impact of a compromised application.

rules.title: AppArmor is enabled in the bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: AppArmor must be enabled at boot through kernel parameters such as apparmor=1 so that profiles are applied from early startup.
rules.impact: If AppArmor is not enabled in the bootloader configuration, confinement profiles may not load before services initialize, leaving processes unrestricted.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce or complain mode
rules.explanation: Loaded AppArmor profiles should be active in enforce mode (restrictions applied) or complain mode (violations logged). Profiles that are unloaded or unconfined provide no protection.
rules.impact: An application running without an active AppArmor profile is not confined and may access resources beyond its intended policy, expanding the impact of compromise.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce mode
rules.explanation: Enforce mode provides the strongest AppArmor protection by blocking policy violations rather than only logging them. This is the recommended mode for production systems.
rules.impact: In complain mode, violations are logged but not blocked. A compromised application can continue to violate policy, allowing an attack to proceed without AppArmor enforcement.

rules.title: A bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: A GRUB bootloader password restricts unauthorized changes to boot parameters and kernel command-line options when physical or local console access is available.
rules.impact: Without a bootloader password, an attacker with console access can alter kernel parameters—for example to disable AppArmor—and bypass security controls.

rules.title: ASLR is enabled
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit mitigation technique that randomly arranges key regions of a process address space.
rules.impact: Disabled or weak ASLR makes memory-corruption exploits significantly easier because attackers can more reliably predict stack, heap, and library locations. Setting kernel.randomize_va_space to 2 enables full randomization.

rules.title: Kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is configured
rules.explanation: The ptrace system call allows one process to observe and control another process, including inspecting and modifying its memory and registers.
rules.impact: If one application is compromised, an attacker may use ptrace to attach to other processes running as the same user and extract additional credentials. Restricting ptrace scope limits lateral movement within a user's process set.

rules.title: Core dumps are restricted
rules.explanation: Core dumps capture process memory at crash time and may contain sensitive data such as credentials, keys, or session material. Limits can be enforced through ulimit settings and kernel.core_pattern.
rules.impact: Unrestricted core dumps increase the risk that sensitive data is written to disk and later disclosed if dump files are readable by unauthorized users.

rules.title: The password hashing algorithm is SHA-512
rules.explanation: Password hashing algorithms protect stored credentials by transforming passwords into irreversible digests. SHA-512 provides substantially stronger resistance to offline cracking than legacy algorithms such as MD5.
rules.impact: Weaker hashing algorithms make offline password cracking more feasible if password hashes are obtained. Using SHA-512 increases the effort required for an attacker to recover passwords from stolen hashes.

rules.title: Automatic error reporting is disabled
rules.explanation: Automatic error-reporting services such as apport may collect crash data that can include environment details, paths, or other sensitive information and transmit it off-host.
rules.impact: Disabling automatic error reporting reduces the risk of unintended disclosure of sensitive system or application data to external services.

rules.title: Kernel.kptr_restrict is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel.kptr_restrict sysctl controls whether kernel addresses are exposed through /proc and other interfaces.
rules.impact: Masking kernel pointers, including symbols visible via /proc/kallsyms, reduces an attacker's ability to gather layout information useful for developing or weaponizing kernel exploits.

rules.title: Kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is configured
rules.explanation: The ptrace system call allows one process to observe and control another process, including inspecting and modifying its memory and registers.
rules.impact: If one application is compromised, an attacker may use ptrace to attach to other processes running as the same user and extract additional credentials. Restricting ptrace scope limits lateral movement within a user's process set.

rules.title: Kernel.randomize_va_space is configured
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit mitigation technique that randomly arranges key regions of a process address space.
rules.impact: Randomizing virtual memory layout makes memory-corruption exploits more difficult to develop and reuse because target addresses change between executions.

rules.title: Systemd-coredump ProcessSizeMax is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump captures the memory of a running process, typically to diagnose crashes. Core files may also contain sensitive information from process memory.
rules.impact: Limiting the maximum process size handled by systemd-coredump reduces retention of large memory images that may contain sensitive data, lowering the risk of information disclosure from core dumps.

rules.title: Core dump file size is limited
rules.explanation: The core resource limit controls the maximum size of core dump files. A hard limit enforces a ceiling that users cannot raise.
rules.impact: A hard limit on core dumps prevents users from overriding a restrictive soft limit. Core dumps capture process memory at termination and may contain sensitive data, so unconstrained dumps increase the risk of information disclosure.

rules.title: /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after successful logon and serve as the message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: A clear message-of-the-day banner communicates acceptable-use policy and legal notice to users after login, supporting accountability and awareness.

rules.title: /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before logon on local terminals.
rules.impact: A local login banner warns console users of authorized-use restrictions before authentication and can support accountability for unauthorized access.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before logon for remote connections from configured network services.
rules.impact: A remote login banner informs network clients of site policy before authentication and can support accountability for unauthorized remote access attempts.

rules.title: The gdm3 package is not installed unless required
rules.explanation: The gdm3 package provides the GNOME Display Manager graphical login service. Servers that do not require a graphical console typically have no need for GDM.
rules.impact: Installing an unused display manager expands the installed software surface and introduces additional services and potential vulnerabilities on systems that should remain headless.

rules.title: Chargen services are not in use
rules.explanation: The chargen (Character Generator) service returns a continuous stream of characters and was historically used for network testing over TCP and UDP.
rules.impact: An enabled chargen service can be abused in reflected denial-of-service attacks and unnecessarily expands the network attack surface.

rules.title: Daytime services are not in use
rules.explanation: The daytime service (TCP/UDP port 13) returns the current system time as plain text. The protocol is obsolete and does not require authentication.
rules.impact: Legacy network services increase the attack surface without providing operational value on modern systems.

rules.title: Discard services are not in use
rules.explanation: The discard service (TCP/UDP port 9) silently discards all received data. It is an obsolete diagnostic service that is not required on modern servers.
rules.impact: Removing unnecessary network services reduces opportunities for denial-of-service abuse and limits exposed listeners.

rules.title: Echo services are not in use
rules.explanation: The echo service (TCP/UDP port 7) returns every received byte to the sender. The protocol is obsolete and can be abused for reflected denial-of-service attacks.
rules.impact: Disabling echo services prevents their use in amplification or reflection attacks and reduces unnecessary network exposure.

rules.title: Legacy time services are not in use
rules.explanation: Legacy time services (distinct from modern NTP clients such as chrony or systemd-timesyncd) expose unauthenticated time protocols that are obsolete on current systems.
rules.impact: Legacy time protocols lack modern authentication and integrity protections and expand the network attack surface without operational benefit.

rules.title: The TFTP service is not in use
rules.explanation: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) provides simple file transfer without authentication or encryption and is commonly exposed via xinetd or a dedicated systemd unit.
rules.impact: A running TFTP service can allow unauthorized file retrieval or planting of files, leading to data exposure or introduction of malicious content.

rules.title: Talk services are not in use
rules.explanation: Talk is a legacy daemon for interactive text messaging between users on a system or network. The protocol does not support encryption.
rules.impact: Unencrypted talk sessions can expose message content and expand the attack surface through an obsolete communication service.

rules.title: The telnet server is not installed
rules.explanation: Telnet provides remote terminal access but transmits session data, including credentials, in cleartext.
rules.impact: Use of Telnet allows credentials and session content to be intercepted on the network. Secure alternatives such as SSH should be used instead.

rules.title: Rsh services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsh family (rlogin, rexec, and related r-services) provides remote command and login access using obsolete, unencrypted host-trust mechanisms.
rules.impact: R-services expose unencrypted remote access paths that can be abused for credential interception and unauthorized host access.

rules.title: The rsync daemon is not in use unless required
rules.explanation: Rsync in daemon mode listens on a network port and can synchronize filesystem content. Without careful configuration it may allow unauthenticated or weakly protected data access.
rules.impact: An exposed rsync daemon is a common source of unauthorized data exposure and can provide a path for remote file retrieval or modification.

rules.title: Print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: CUPS provides printing services. On servers without printers it is unnecessary and expands the installed service surface. CUPS has been associated with serious remote vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: Vulnerabilities in CUPS (including CVE-2024-47076 and related issues) have enabled unauthenticated remote code execution. An unnecessary print service creates a critical network attack vector.

rules.title: Rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: rpcbind maps Remote Procedure Call (RPC) services to the ports on which they listen and redirects clients to the correct port. Portmapper is the related RPC service used for this mapping.
rules.impact: Portmapper responses can be abused in amplification-style DDoS attacks. If RPC port mapping is not required, removing rpcbind reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: Rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsyncd service synchronizes files between systems over network connections.
rules.impact: rsyncd commonly communicates without encryption, exposing transferred data and increasing risk if the daemon is reachable. If the service is not required, removing the rsync-daemon package reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: Samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon enables Linux systems to share filesystems and directories with Windows clients using SMB/CIFS protocols.
rules.impact: If Windows file sharing is not required, removing Samba reduces the attack surface associated with an unused network file server.

rules.title: SNMP services are not in use
rules.explanation: SNMP is a protocol commonly used to monitor network equipment, hosts, and devices such as UPS units.
rules.impact: SNMP servers may support SNMPv1, which transmits data in cleartext and offers weak authentication. If SNMP is not required, removing net-snmp reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: TFTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: TFTP is a simple file-transfer protocol used between TCP/IP hosts. A TFTP server allows clients to send and receive files with minimal protocol overhead.
rules.impact: TFTP provides no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. If the system is not required to operate as a TFTP server, removing the package reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: Web proxy server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Squid is a widely used HTTP/HTTPS caching proxy server packaged in many Linux distributions.
rules.impact: Unless the system is intentionally configured as a proxy server, retaining Squid increases the attack surface of an unused network service.

rules.title: Web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web server packages provide the ability to host and serve website or application content over HTTP and related protocols.
rules.impact: If there is no approved requirement to run a web server on the system, removing web server packages reduces the network-facing attack surface.

rules.title: Xinetd services are not in use
rules.explanation: xinetd is a super-server that listens for network connections and starts the corresponding service on demand. Many legacy services historically relied on xinetd.
rules.impact: Removing unused xinetd deployments reduces the number of network listeners and associated vulnerabilities on the host.

rules.title: X Window System services are not in use
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical user interface in which users can run applications in multiple windows and related desktop components.
rules.impact: If graphical logon and X Window access are not required by organizational policy, removing these services reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: A Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) such as Postfix or sendmail should accept mail only from the local host (127.0.0.1/::1) when the system is not intended to be a network mail server.
rules.impact: An MTA listening on external interfaces can be abused as an open relay for spam or phishing and expands the attack surface on mail protocols.

rules.title: Only approved services listen on network interfaces
rules.explanation: Network-facing services should be limited to those required by the system role. Unexpected listeners indicate misconfiguration or unauthorized software.
rules.impact: Unnecessary listening services increase remote attack surface and may expose management interfaces or vulnerable application endpoints to the network.

rules.title: Ypserv is not in use
rules.explanation: ypserv provides NIS (Network Information Service) server functionality for distributing account and configuration maps to NIS clients.
rules.impact: NIS does not protect credentials in transit and is vulnerable to interception and spoofing. Unused NIS server components should be removed to reduce that exposure.

rules.title: Ypbind is not installed
rules.explanation: ypbind is the NIS client daemon that binds a host to an NIS domain for distributed account and configuration lookups.
rules.impact: NIS traffic is unencrypted; retaining ypbind when NIS is not required increases the risk of credential exposure and expands unused client attack surface.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed
rules.explanation: The rsh client tools enable use of obsolete remote shell protocols that transmit data without encryption.
rules.impact: Presence of the rsh client increases the likelihood of insecure remote access and credential exposure, and can bypass policies that require SSH.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed
rules.explanation: The talk client is a legacy program for interactive network messaging that does not encrypt communications.
rules.impact: Legacy talk protocols expose message content to interception and provide no security benefit on modern systems.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet package provides a client that establishes interactive remote sessions using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: Telnet is unencrypted, so credentials and session data can be intercepted on the network. Encrypted alternatives such as SSH provide stronger protection, and removing an unused telnet client reduces risk.

rules.title: The LDAP client is not installed
rules.explanation: LDAP provides a method for looking up directory information in a central database and historically replaced NIS/YP for many environments.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to act as an LDAP client, removing the client software reduces the attack surface of unused directory-access tooling.

rules.title: Time synchronization is in use
rules.explanation: System clocks should be synchronized across hosts in an environment. This is typically achieved by using one or more authoritative time sources and configuring all systems to follow them.
rules.impact: Accurate time supports security mechanisms such as Kerberos and produces consistent log timestamps across systems, which is essential for correlation and forensic investigation.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is enabled and active
rules.explanation: When systemd-timesyncd is the selected NTP client, the service must be enabled at boot and running so that the system clock remains synchronized.
rules.impact: Without continuous time synchronization, clock drift can break Kerberos authentication, undermine log correlation, and cause TLS certificate validation failures.

rules.title: Chrony is not running as the root user
rules.explanation: chronyd should run as an unprivileged user such as _chrony rather than as root, following least privilege for system daemons.
rules.impact: Running chronyd as root means that exploitation of an NTP-related vulnerability could yield full superuser privileges on the host.

rules.title: Chrony is enabled and active
rules.explanation: When chrony is the selected NTP client, the chronyd service must be enabled at boot and running to maintain continuous clock synchronization.
rules.impact: A non-functioning NTP client allows system time to drift, which can break PKI certificate validation, Kerberos authentication, and correlation of security events.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon schedules and executes batch jobs on the system according to configured schedules.
rules.impact: Even when user jobs are uncommon, systems rely on scheduled maintenance and security-monitoring tasks. An inactive cron daemon can prevent those controls from running as intended.

rules.title: IP forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The parameters net.ipv4.ip_forward and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding control whether the system may forward packets between network interfaces.
rules.impact: IP forwarding is appropriate for routers but unnecessary on most hosts. Leaving forwarding enabled can allow the host to route traffic unexpectedly and expand exposure of adjacent networks.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology used to exchange data between nearby devices.
rules.impact: Unused Bluetooth services can expose systems to unauthorized proximity-based access and malware propagation between paired or discoverable devices, increasing the attack surface.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: Source routing allows a packet sender to specify the path taken through the network. The parameters net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route control whether such packets are accepted.
rules.impact: Accepting source-routed packets can enable attackers to bypass network filters and reach otherwise inaccessible systems.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages instruct a host to use an alternate route. The parameters net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects control whether redirects are accepted.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP redirects allows external hosts to influence system routing and can divert traffic through attacker-controlled paths.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are ICMP redirects that originate from gateways listed in the default gateway list. net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects controls whether these redirects are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Even known gateways may be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 prevents routing-table updates from potentially untrusted gateways.

rules.title: Martian packets are logged
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with impossible or non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log for all interfaces.
rules.impact: Logging martian packets helps administrators detect spoofed or malformed traffic that may indicate reconnaissance or attack activity against the system.

rules.title: Broadcast ICMP echoes are ignored
rules.explanation: The parameter net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts controls whether the host responds to ICMP echo and timestamp requests sent to broadcast or multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Responding to broadcast ICMP echoes can be abused in Smurf-style denial-of-service attacks that amplify traffic toward a spoofed victim.

rules.title: Bogus ICMP error responses are ignored
rules.explanation: The parameter net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses controls whether the kernel ignores ICMP error messages that violate RFC expectations.
rules.impact: Processing bogus ICMP error responses can clutter logs and may disrupt network communication; ignoring them reduces noise and related abuse.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.ip_forward is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward parameter controls whether the system may forward IPv4 packets between network interfaces.
rules.impact: IP forwarding is appropriate for routers but unnecessary on most hosts. Leaving forwarding enabled can expose or advertise network topology and allow the host to route traffic unexpectedly. Setting net.ipv4.ip_forward to 0 prevents a multi-interface system from forwarding IPv4 packets.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding controls IPv4 packet forwarding across all network interfaces.
rules.impact: Forwarding capabilities are typically reserved for routers that exchange topology information with other routers. Enabling forwarding when it is not required can cause the system to participate in routing unexpectedly and expose network information.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding controls IPv4 packet forwarding for newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Forwarding capabilities are typically reserved for routers. Enabling default forwarding when it is not required can cause newly added interfaces to route traffic unexpectedly and expose network information.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects controls whether IPv4 ICMP Redirect messages are sent on all network interfaces.
rules.impact: A compromised host can send forged ICMP redirects to manipulate routing decisions and divert users to attacker-controlled systems instead of legitimate destinations.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects controls whether IPv4 ICMP Redirect messages are sent on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: A compromised host can send forged ICMP redirects to manipulate routing decisions and divert users to attacker-controlled systems instead of legitimate destinations.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses controls whether the kernel logs or ignores ICMP error responses that do not match RFC-1122 expectations.
rules.impact: Some routers and attackers send invalid ICMP replies that can flood logs with useless error messages. Ignoring bogus responses reduces log noise and related disruption.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts controls whether ICMP echo and timestamp requests to broadcast and multicast addresses are ignored.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP echoes to broadcast or multicast destinations can be used to enlist the host in a Smurf attack, amplifying traffic toward a spoofed source address.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages convey alternate-path routing information to hosts. net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects controls whether IPv4 ICMP Redirect packets are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP redirects allows external hosts to influence the system routing table. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0 prevents unsolicited updates that could redirect traffic through attacker-controlled paths.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects controls whether IPv4 ICMP Redirect packets are accepted on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP redirects on new interfaces allows external hosts to influence routing. Setting this parameter to 0 prevents unsolicited routing-table updates on those interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are ICMP redirects that originate from gateways listed in the default gateway list. net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects controls whether these redirects are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Even known gateways may be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 prevents routing-table updates from potentially untrusted gateways.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects originate from gateways listed in the default gateway list. net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects controls whether they are accepted on newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: Even known gateways may be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects to 0 prevents routing-table updates from potentially untrusted gateways on new interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on all network interfaces, verifying that inbound packets arrive on an expected interface for their source address.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter to 1 helps drop spoofed packets that would not be answerable via the receiving path. Note that asymmetric routing environments may require careful evaluation of this setting.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 helps prevent acceptance of spoofed packets that would not be answerable via the receiving path on new interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route controls whether IPv4 packets with Strict or Loose Source Routing options are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Source-routed packets can bypass intended routing and filtering. Disabling acceptance of source routes prevents attackers from specifying arbitrary paths through the host.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route controls whether IPv4 packets with Strict or Loose Source Routing options are accepted on newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling source routing on new interfaces prevents attackers from using source-routed packets to reach otherwise inaccessible networks through the host.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with impossible or non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log for all interfaces.
rules.impact: Logging martian packets helps administrators detect spoofed or malformed traffic that may indicate reconnaissance or attack activity against the system.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with impossible or non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log for newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: Logging martian packets on new interfaces helps administrators detect spoofed or malformed traffic that may indicate reconnaissance or attack activity.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is configured
rules.explanation: When tcp_syncookies is enabled, the kernel handles TCP SYN packets normally until the connection queue is full, after which SYN cookie handling protects new connection attempts.
rules.impact: SYN flood attacks exhaust connection queues by sending many SYN packets without completing the handshake. Enabling SYN cookies allows the system to continue accepting legitimate connections during denial-of-service conditions.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding parameter controls whether the system may forward IPv6 packets between network interfaces.
rules.impact: IPv6 forwarding is appropriate for routers but unnecessary on most hosts. Leaving it enabled can expose network topology and allow unexpected routing. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding to 0 prevents a multi-interface system from forwarding IPv6 packets.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding parameter controls whether newly added or default network interfaces may forward IPv6 packets.
rules.impact: IPv6 forwarding is typically reserved for routers. Enabling it when not required can cause the system to advertise or route network information unexpectedly.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects controls whether IPv6 ICMP Redirect packets are accepted on all network interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting IPv6 redirects allows external hosts to influence system routing. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0 prevents outsiders from updating the routing table through redirect messages.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects controls whether IPv6 ICMP Redirect packets are accepted on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting IPv6 redirects on new interfaces allows external hosts to influence routing. Setting this parameter to 0 prevents unsolicited routing-table updates.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route controls whether IPv6 packets with source-routing options are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling IPv6 source routing prevents attackers from specifying packet paths that bypass intended network controls.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route controls whether IPv6 packets with source-routing options are accepted on newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling IPv6 source routing on new interfaces reduces the risk that source-routed packets are used to reach otherwise inaccessible systems.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send multicast Router Advertisement (RA) messages to announce availability and provide autoconfiguration information to neighboring nodes. net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra controls whether these messages are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting unsolicited router advertisements can cause a host to route traffic through attacker-controlled systems. Disabling RA acceptance reduces the risk of malicious network reconfiguration.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send multicast Router Advertisement (RA) messages to announce availability and provide autoconfiguration information. net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra controls whether these messages are accepted on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting unsolicited router advertisements can cause a host to route traffic through attacker-controlled systems. Disabling RA acceptance on new interfaces reduces the risk of malicious network reconfiguration.

rules.title: The auditd service is installed and active
rules.explanation: auditd is the userspace component of the Linux audit subsystem and writes audit records to disk. Installing the audit packages provides the daemon and related tools needed for system event auditing.
rules.impact: Without auditd, administrators lack durable records of security-relevant system events needed to detect and investigate unauthorized access or policy violations.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon records security-relevant system events according to configured audit rules. Enabling and activating the service ensures auditing starts at boot and continues during operation.
rules.impact: If auditd is not enabled to start at boot, auditing will not begin until the service is started manually, creating a gap in the security event trail after reboot.

rules.title: Auditing for processes that start prior to auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter audit=1 enables auditing during early boot, before the auditd daemon is fully started, so that initialization events are captured.
rules.impact: Without early auditing, actions that occur before auditd starts—including potentially malicious modifications during boot—may not be recorded.

rules.title: Audit_backlog_limit is configured
rules.explanation: The audit_backlog_limit kernel parameter sets how many pending audit records can be held in the audit queue. An adequate limit is especially important early in boot when audit=1 may be enabled before auditd is fully ready.
rules.impact: If the backlog is too small during boot, audit records can be dropped, allowing potentially malicious activity to go unrecorded.

rules.title: Audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: auditd allows configuration of the maximum size of audit log files. Setting an appropriate max_log_file value balances retention needs against available disk capacity.
rules.impact: Without a defined maximum size, audit logs may grow until they impact system stability, or rotation behavior may be undefined, increasing the risk of lost or incomplete audit data.

rules.title: Password length and complexity are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/pwquality.conf settings define minimum password length and character-class requirements for new passwords.
rules.impact: Weak password requirements make credentials easier to guess or crack. Enforcing sufficient length and character diversity increases resistance to password attacks.

rules.title: Account lockout after failed attempts is configured
rules.explanation: The faillock settings deny and unlock_time define how many consecutive failed logons trigger a lock and how long the account remains locked.
rules.impact: Without lockout controls, online password-guessing attacks can proceed without throttling, increasing the likelihood of credential compromise.

rules.title: ENCRYPT_METHOD is set to SHA512
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs defines the default algorithm used to hash new user passwords. SHA-512 provides strong resistance to offline cracking compared with legacy methods.
rules.impact: Legacy hashing methods such as MD5 or DES make offline password cracking far more feasible if password hashes are obtained.

rules.title: Sshd access is configured
rules.explanation: OpenSSH provides directives such as AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, and DenyGroups to restrict which users and groups may authenticate to the SSH service.
rules.impact: Without access restrictions, any valid local account may attempt remote SSH login. Limiting SSH access to authorized users and groups reduces the risk of unauthorized remote access and narrows the attack surface.

rules.title: Sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents are displayed to the remote client before authentication is allowed.
rules.impact: A pre-login banner communicates site-specific connection and acceptable-use policy to connecting users. Displaying a legal warning before authentication can support accountability and assist in prosecuting unauthorized access.

rules.title: Sshd Ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: The Ciphers directive restricts which symmetric encryption algorithms SSH may negotiate for protecting session confidentiality.
rules.impact: Weak or outdated ciphers may fail to provide adequate confidentiality or integrity for SSH sessions. Restricting SSH to strong ciphers reduces the risk that session data can be intercepted or altered.

rules.title: Sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control how the SSH server detects and terminates idle or unresponsive client sessions through keepalive messages.
rules.impact: Sessions left open indefinitely consume resources and may be hijacked if a user leaves a connection unattended. Appropriate timeout values reduce the risk of resource exhaustion and limit the window for unauthorized use of abandoned sessions.

rules.title: Sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: The DisableForwarding parameter disables all SSH forwarding features, including X11 forwarding, ssh-agent forwarding, TCP forwarding, and StreamLocal forwarding.
rules.impact: Forwarding features can be abused to tunnel traffic through the SSH host, bypass network controls, or establish covert channels. Disabling forwarding reduces the attack surface unless a documented operational need exists.

rules.title: Sshd GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The GSSAPIAuthentication parameter controls whether users may authenticate to SSH using GSSAPI-based mechanisms such as Kerberos.
rules.impact: Enabling GSSAPI authentication exposes additional authentication pathways from remote hosts. Disabling it when not required reduces the system attack surface and limits dependency on external authentication infrastructure.

rules.title: Sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication permits authentication based on trusted hosts using mechanisms historically associated with .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv style trust.
rules.impact: Host-based authentication is weaker than user-centric methods and can be abused if host trust relationships are compromised. Disabling it provides defense in depth even when related PAM or rhosts support is already limited.

rules.title: Sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter causes sshd to ignore .rhosts and .shosts files during RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Ignoring .rhosts and .shosts files prevents weak host-trust based authentication paths from being used. This reduces the risk of unauthorized access through manipulated or legacy trust files.

rules.title: Sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: KexAlgorithms defines the key exchange methods SSH may use to establish shared session keys between client and server before encrypted communication begins.
rules.impact: Weak key exchange algorithms—those with insufficient key strength or weak hash functions—can expose SSH sessions to man-in-the-middle and related cryptographic attacks. Restricting KexAlgorithms to strong methods protects the integrity of the handshake.

rules.title: Sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime specifies how long the SSH server allows a connection to remain unauthenticated before disconnecting the client.
rules.impact: A long grace period increases the opportunity for brute-force authentication attempts and can allow many concurrent unauthenticated connections. A reasonably short LoginGraceTime reduces these risks and limits resource consumption by incomplete logins.

rules.title: Sshd LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: LogLevel controls the verbosity of OpenSSH server logging, ranging from minimal messages to detailed diagnostic output.
rules.impact: Adequate SSH logging supports detection and investigation of unauthorized access attempts. Levels such as INFO or VERBOSE capture login activity—and at VERBOSE, key fingerprints used for authentication—improving auditability without excessive noise.

rules.title: Sshd MACs are configured
rules.explanation: The MACs directive restricts which message authentication code algorithms SSH may use to protect the integrity of encrypted session data.
rules.impact: Weak MAC algorithms, including MD5-based and 96-bit MACs, have been associated with SSH downgrade and related cryptographic attacks. Restricting MACs to strong algorithms reduces the risk of session tampering and cryptographic compromise.

rules.title: Sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted per SSH connection before the connection is terminated.
rules.impact: Unlimited or high authentication attempt limits facilitate password guessing and brute-force attacks against SSH. A low MaxAuthTries value reduces the effectiveness of such attacks per connection.

rules.title: Sshd MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions specifies the maximum number of open sessions permitted for a single SSH connection.
rules.impact: Excessive concurrent sessions on a single connection can consume resources and contribute to denial of service. Limiting MaxSessions helps preserve sshd availability and prevent daemon overload.

rules.title: Sshd MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: MaxStartups limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections that the SSH daemon will accept, with optional rate-limiting behavior as connections approach the limit.
rules.impact: A flood of unauthenticated SSH connections can exhaust resources and degrade or deny legitimate login availability. Configuring MaxStartups mitigates denial-of-service risk against sshd.

rules.title: Sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitEmptyPasswords controls whether the SSH server allows login to accounts that have an empty password string.
rules.impact: Accounts with empty passwords can be accessed without credentials, enabling trivial unauthorized remote access. Disabling PermitEmptyPasswords reduces the likelihood of unauthenticated shell access via SSH.

rules.title: Sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitRootLogin controls whether the root account may authenticate directly over SSH.
rules.impact: Direct root SSH logins obscure individual accountability and concentrate risk on a single privileged credential. Requiring administrators to log in with individual accounts and then escalate privileges improves non-repudiation and audit trails during security incidents.

rules.title: Sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitUserEnvironment allows users to set environment variables for their SSH sessions via environment files processed by the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: User-controlled environment variables passed through sshd can be used to alter program behavior and potentially bypass security controls. Disabling this option reduces that risk.

rules.title: Sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) interface for SSH authentication, account, and session management.
rules.impact: When UsePAM is enabled, SSH leverages system PAM policy for account and session handling, ensuring consistent enforcement of local authentication controls such as lockouts and password policies.

rules.title: Sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) interface for SSH authentication, account, and session management.
rules.impact: When UsePAM is enabled, SSH leverages system PAM policy for account and session handling, ensuring consistent enforcement of local authentication controls such as lockouts and password policies.

rules.title: Root login is restricted to authorized terminals
rules.explanation: The /etc/securetty file lists terminals from which the root account may log in. Restricting this list limits where direct root console authentication is permitted.
rules.impact: Unrestricted root login paths increase the chance of unauthorized privileged access from unexpected terminals or local attack surfaces.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a shell or command as another user. By default, any local user may attempt to invoke su.
rules.impact: Unrestricted su use enables broader attempts to obtain other accounts' privileges, including root. Restricting su—typically in favor of sudo—gives administrators stronger control over privilege elevation.

rules.title: Access to SSH host public key files is configured
rules.explanation: SSH host public key files correspond to the host private keys and are presented to clients during the SSH handshake to verify the server identity.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of host public key files can disrupt SSH trust relationships or facilitate host impersonation. Protecting these files reduces the risk of SSH service compromise through key tampering.

rules.title: Users must provide a password for privilege escalation
rules.explanation: The system must require users to authenticate with a password when elevating privileges through mechanisms such as sudo, rather than allowing passwordless escalation.
rules.impact: Without reauthentication at privilege escalation, an unattended or compromised user session may be used to perform unauthorized administrative actions. Requiring a password reduces that risk and reinforces accountability.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: A global !authenticate (or equivalent) setting in sudoers disables authentication for privilege escalation across users, undermining sudo's confirmation of identity.
rules.impact: Globally disabling sudo authentication allows any authorized sudo user to obtain elevated privileges without a password, so a compromised user session immediately yields administrative access.

rules.title: Sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) interface for SSH authentication, account, and session management.
rules.impact: When UsePAM is enabled, SSH leverages system PAM policy for account and session handling, ensuring consistent enforcement of local authentication controls such as lockouts and password policies.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a shell or command as another user. By default, any local user may attempt to invoke su.
rules.impact: Unrestricted su use enables broader attempts to obtain other accounts' privileges, including root. Restricting su—typically in favor of sudo—gives administrators stronger control over privilege elevation.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/pam.d/su: pam_wheel.so, and group in /etc/group

rules.title: Lockout includes the root account
rules.explanation: Account lockout after failed authentication should apply to the root account as well as ordinary users so that privileged credentials are not exempt from brute-force protections.
rules.impact: Excluding root from lockout allows unlimited password-guessing against the most privileged account on the system.

rules.title: The minimum number of changed characters in a password is configured
rules.explanation: Password quality settings can require that a new password differ from the old password by a minimum number of characters, reducing trivial rotations.
rules.impact: Requiring meaningful character changes makes it harder for users to recycle nearly identical passwords after a forced change.

rules.title: Password length is configured
rules.explanation: The minlen parameter sets the minimum acceptable length for a new password during password quality checks.
rules.impact: Short passwords are significantly easier to compromise through guessing and brute-force attacks. Enforcing a minimum length strengthens resistance to credential attacks.

rules.title: Password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: Password complexity requirements can be enforced using parameters such as minclass, dcredit, ucredit, ocredit, and lcredit to require diverse character classes in new passwords.
rules.impact: Passwords lacking character diversity are more susceptible to brute-force and dictionary attacks. Enforcing complexity requirements increases password strength and reduces the likelihood of successful credential compromise.

rules.title: Repeating character restrictions are configured
rules.explanation: Password quality modules can reject passwords that contain too many consecutive identical characters, which are easier to guess.
rules.impact: Restricting repeated characters reduces the chance that users select predictable passwords that weaken account security.

rules.title: Consecutive character sequence restrictions are configured
rules.explanation: Password quality modules can reject passwords that contain sequential character runs such as numeric or alphabetic sequences.
rules.impact: Blocking common sequences reduces password predictability and strengthens resistance to guessing and dictionary-style attacks.

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: The dictcheck parameter controls whether candidate passwords are checked against the cracklib dictionary of common or weak words.
rules.impact: Dictionary-based passwords are frequently targeted in guessing and brute-force attacks. Enabling dictionary checking reduces the chance that users select easily cracked passwords.

rules.title: Password quality checking is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module performs password quality checking when users set or change passwords, enforcing complexity and related strength requirements.
rules.impact: Weak passwords are easier to guess or crack. Enforcing password quality increases the time and resources required for successful password attacks and improves overall account security.

rules.title: Password quality is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: When enforce_for_root is enabled, pam_pwquality returns an error on failed quality checks even when the password being changed belongs to the root account.
rules.impact: Weak root passwords present a high-impact risk because root controls the entire system. Enforcing password quality for root increases the effort required to crack the privileged credential.

rules.title: Password history remembering is configured
rules.explanation: Previous passwords are stored in /etc/security/opasswd and checked to prevent reuse. The remember argument sets how many prior passwords are retained for history enforcement.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse recent passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can reuse a guessed or previously compromised password after a password change.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option forces pam_pwhistory, when changing a password, to use the new password already provided by a previously stacked password module rather than prompting again.
rules.impact: use_authtok ensures password modules in the PAM stack operate on the same confirmed new password, preserving consistent enforcement of history and quality checks before the password is accepted.
rules.scope: File: /etc/pam.d/common-password, line: password required pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides the default pam_unix.so behavior that denies access when a user's password is empty, allowing authentication with a blank password.
rules.impact: Empty passwords provide no authentication strength and enable unauthorized access. Removing nullok helps ensure that accounts cannot authenticate without a password.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: The remember=n argument to pam_unix stores the last n passwords in /etc/security/opasswd for history checking. Password history should be handled by pam_pwhistory rather than pam_unix.
rules.impact: Using remember with pam_unix can interfere with strong password hashing and duplicates history functionality better provided by pam_pwhistory. Removing remember from pam_unix supports proper hashing and cleaner PAM configuration.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: The pam_unix module should be configured to use a strong password hashing algorithm such as SHA-512 when updating local credentials.
rules.impact: Weak hashing algorithms make offline cracking of stolen password hashes significantly easier and undermine account security if the credential store is disclosed.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option forces pam_unix, when changing a password, to use the new password provided by a previously stacked password module rather than prompting independently.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows stacked PAM modules to validate and confirm the same new password before it is committed, ensuring quality and history checks are applied consistently.
rules.scope: File: /etc/pam.d/common-password, line: password required pam_unix.so use_authtok

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0 as primary group
rules.explanation: GID 0 identifies the privileged root group. The root account's primary group membership should be GID 0, and ordinary accounts should not use GID 0 as their primary group.
rules.impact: Assigning GID 0 as a primary group to non-root accounts can grant unintended access to root-group-owned files. Keeping GID 0 associated with root helps prevent accidental or unauthorized privileged group access.

rules.title: Root is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: GID 0 is reserved for the root group. No other group should be assigned GID 0.
rules.impact: Duplicate GID 0 groups can create ambiguous ownership and unintended access to files owned by the root group. Ensuring only the root group uses GID 0 reduces the risk of privileged group access by unprivileged users.

rules.title: The root password is set
rules.explanation: The root account should have a password configured so that privileged local authentication cannot succeed with an empty credential.
rules.impact: A root account without a password may allow unauthorized privileged access depending on authentication configuration, creating a critical exposure.

rules.title: Root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask (user file-creation mode mask) determines the default permission bits removed when the root user creates new files and directories.
rules.impact: An overly permissive root umask can create world- or group-writable sensitive files by default. A secure umask reduces accidental exposure of privileged files and directories.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: System accounts used by services should use a non-login shell such as /usr/sbin/nologin so they cannot be used for interactive logon.
rules.impact: A valid shell on a system account increases the risk that the account is used for interactive access if its credentials are compromised.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Accounts configured with a non-login shell should also be locked so that they cannot authenticate through other access paths.
rules.impact: Unlocked accounts without interactive shells may still be usable for some authentication methods; locking them reduces unauthorized access risk.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists full paths of shells considered valid for user login. Utilities such as chsh consult this file when changing a user's shell.
rules.impact: If nologin is listed in /etc/shells, accounts configured with nologin may be treated as having a valid interactive shell. Removing nologin from /etc/shells helps ensure non-login accounts remain non-interactive.

rules.title: Password maximum lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs defines the maximum number of days a password may be used before it must be changed.
rules.impact: Limiting password lifetime reduces the window during which a compromised or guessed credential remains valid. Periodic expiration also limits prolonged use of weak or exposed passwords.

rules.title: Password expiration warning days are configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs specifies how many days before password expiration users are warned that their password will expire.
rules.impact: Advance notice of password expiration gives users time to choose a strong replacement password and reduces rushed or weak password changes that can undermine account security.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs defines the default algorithm used to hash user passwords stored by the system.
rules.impact: Weaker hashing algorithms make offline password cracking more feasible if password hashes are obtained. SHA-512 and yescrypt provide stronger resistance to password cracking than legacy Linux hashing methods.

rules.title: Inactive password lock is configured
rules.explanation: INACTIVE defines the number of days after a password has expired during which the user may still log in and change the password before the account is locked for inactivity.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts are less likely to be monitored for failed logons or other anomalies and may retain valid credentials unused for long periods. Locking inactive accounts reduces the risk that dormant credentials are abused.

rules.title: Last password change date is in the past for all users
rules.explanation: Each user account records the date of the last password change. That date must be in the past for password aging policies to apply correctly.
rules.impact: A last password change date set in the future can cause password expiration controls to be bypassed or delayed. Ensuring dates are in the past preserves the effectiveness of configured password lifetime policies.

rules.title: Root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: Any account with UID 0 has unrestricted superuser privileges on the system, equivalent to the root account.
rules.impact: Multiple UID 0 accounts expand the set of credentials that grant full system control and complicate accountability. Restricting UID 0 to root reduces privilege sprawl and the risk of unauthorized superuser access.

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0 as primary group
rules.explanation: GID 0 identifies the privileged root group. The root account's primary group membership should be GID 0, and ordinary accounts should not use GID 0 as their primary group.
rules.impact: Assigning GID 0 as a primary group to non-root accounts can grant unintended access to root-group-owned files. Keeping GID 0 associated with root helps prevent accidental or unauthorized privileged group access.

rules.title: Root is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: GID 0 is reserved for the root group. No other group should be assigned GID 0.
rules.impact: Duplicate GID 0 groups can create ambiguous ownership and unintended access to files owned by the root group. Ensuring only the root group uses GID 0 reduces the risk of privileged group access by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Root PATH integrity is configured
rules.explanation: The root user's PATH must not contain the current directory (.) or empty elements, and directories in PATH should be owned by root and not writable by other users.
rules.impact: Including '.' or writable directories in root's PATH allows an attacker to place a malicious binary that can be executed in place of a system command when run as root.

rules.title: Root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask (user file-creation mode mask) determines the default permission bits removed when the root user creates new files and directories.
rules.impact: An overly permissive root umask can create world- or group-writable sensitive files by default. A secure umask reduces accidental exposure of privileged files and directories.
rules.scope: Files /etc/profile, /etc/bashrc, or the root user shell settings.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: System accounts (for example bin or daemon) must not be assigned an interactive login shell such as /bin/bash.
rules.impact: Preventing interactive shells on system accounts reduces the risk that service accounts are used for logon if compromised.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Accounts that use a non-login shell should be locked to prevent authentication through alternate services.
rules.impact: Locking non-interactive accounts reduces unauthorized use of dormant or service identities.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists full paths of shells considered valid for user login. Utilities such as chsh consult this file when changing a user's shell.
rules.impact: If nologin is listed in /etc/shells, accounts configured with nologin may be treated as having a valid interactive shell. Removing nologin from /etc/shells helps ensure non-login accounts remain non-interactive.

rules.title: Default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The TMOUT variable sets how long a shell may remain idle before the session is terminated automatically.
rules.impact: Without a shell timeout, an abandoned terminal session can remain active indefinitely and may be abused by anyone with access to that session.

rules.title: Default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask (user file-creation mode mask) determines the default permission bits removed when users create new files and directories.
rules.impact: A permissive default umask can cause newly created files to be readable or writable by unintended users. A secure default umask reduces accidental information disclosure and unauthorized modification.

rules.title: Journald service is active
rules.explanation: The systemd-journald service collects and stores system and service log events in the systemd journal. Enabling and activating the service ensures logging begins at boot and continues during normal operation.
